context_blurb:
Burn a match, and its wood is gone for good; snap a glass rod, and every piece is still glass. Chemists sort every change in matter into two kinds, physical and chemical, by one test: has a new substance formed? Flashes and heat can fool the eye; the proof is in what is left.

A physical change alters a substance's shape, size or state, but the substance stays the same. A chemical change, or chemical reaction, turns substances into new ones with new properties, as atoms break their old bonds and form new ones.

Many people believe a change that is impossible to reverse has to be chemical, and they are wrong. A dropped beaker may never be whole again, yet every broken piece is still the same glass, so shattering is only a physical change. Melted down, broken glass makes new glass. Dissolving is physical too, and the proof is easy to try. Stir salt into water until it vanishes, then let the water dry away, and the same salt is left behind: it was there all along, in bits too small to see. An unchanged weight proves nothing, since mass is kept in every change, chemical ones included.

A new property is no proof either. Rub a magnet along an iron nail, always the same way, many times over, and the nail starts lifting paper clips. Iron holds tiny groups of atoms called domains, and stroking lines up their magnetism. No new substance forms, and the nail is still the same iron, so magnetizing it is a physical change. Light and heat are only clues as well. In an old-style bulb, a current heats a thin tungsten wire until it glows. Yet the wire stays tungsten the whole time it glows, and it is still tungsten when it cools, so the glow is a physical change. It cannot burn, because the bulb holds no air, only a vacuum or an unreactive gas.

Burning, though, is chemical. When a match burns down, its wood becomes carbon dioxide, water vapour and ash, and the black stick left is charcoal, mostly carbon: the wood has become new substances, which no change of shape or size could turn back into wood. A firework's black powder burns in a flash into new substances: mostly solid potassium salts, which hang in the sky as white smoke, and hot gases, chiefly carbon dioxide and nitrogen, whose sudden rush bursts the shell.

Even iron can burn. When a 9-volt battery touches fine steel wool, which is almost pure iron, its hair-thin threads glow, spark and leave a dark, crumbly lump. A nail rusting in the wet goes through the same kind of change, only far slower: in both, iron joins with oxygen from the air and becomes iron oxide. The dry wool takes seconds; the wet nail takes months, with no flame or light. Old silver slowly grows a black film of tarnish, but not from oxygen. Traces of sulfur gases in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide given off by wool and rubber, join their sulfur to the silver and make black silver sulfide, a new substance. Because the film is partly made of the silver itself, every polishing carries a little silver away.

Rocks change both ways as they weather, or slowly break down. Water freezing in a crack pries rock apart, but the pieces are the same minerals as before: physical weathering. Carbon dioxide from the air makes rainwater a weak acid, and over many years it reacts with the feldspar crystals in granite and turns them into kaolinite, a soft, white clay mineral that is easy to shape when damp. A new mineral means chemical weathering.

A candle shows both kinds of change at once, and Michael Faraday made it famous in his Christmas Lectures for young audiences at London's Royal Institution. The flame melts the wax, the liquid creeps up the wick, and the heat turns it to gas: changes of state, so the wax stays wax and can still burn. Only the burning is chemical, making carbon dioxide and water vapour, which cannot burn. Faraday showed where the fuel is: he blew a candle out, brought a light into the thin trail drifting up from the wick, and a flame raced down the trail and relit it. The trail was wax turned into a gas, the true fuel of every candle flame.
